Ryser’s Formula

VP ≠ VNPCountingAlgorithms
Game: Find the permanent of a square, which adds up all of its rook products, using a clever shortcut that needs far fewer products.
How to play: Press Next term to add one line at a time and watch the running total. Change the size, or get a new square.
columnsrow sumstermtotal

Look for the math

The permanent adds n! products. In 1963 Herbert Ryser found a way with only 2ⁿ terms, one for each set of columns. It is still the fastest general method known.

perm(A) = (−1)ⁿ ∑S (−1)|S| ∏i (∑j∈S aij)

Too much, then take some back

Multiply out the row sums for a set S of columns. You get every way to pick one entry from each row using columns in S, repeats allowed. The full set gives every pick, including ones that use a column twice. Subtract the picks that avoid one column, add back those that avoid two, and so on. That is inclusion–exclusion. What survives are the picks that use every column, and since there are n rows, each column exactly once: the rook products of the permanent.

Faster, but still exponential

With n − 1 multiplications per term, Ryser needs about n·2ⁿ multiplications against n·n!. That is 9,207 against 32,659,200 at n = 10. But 2ⁿ still doubles with every extra row. Compare the determinant's n³/3: VP ≠ VNP says, roughly, that no circuit for the permanent can be anywhere near that small. The logic test checked Ryser's formula against the full sum on 600 matrices, and the inclusion–exclusion count itself.

Watch the 3 × 3 total: the three single columns and the three pairs overshoot and undershoot before the last term lands on the permanent.
